candidates.text: ICP’s Incubator is located on ICP’s ground floor. The space is free and open to the public during café and museum hours. Since 2018, photographer Melissa Ann Pinney has documented Chicago Public School students as part of an artist residency. As the students began to invite her into their world, the project became a document of identity, community and urgent social issues. Pinney’s thoughtful portraits of young people navigating the transformations of adolescence contain all of the triumph, grief, humor, and tenderness of growing up. About The ArtistMelissa Ann Pinney’s work first garnered attention in the Museum of Modern Art’s major 1991 exhibition, Pleasures and Terrors of Domestic Comfort. Her studies of the social lives and emerging identities of American adolescents have earned her many awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, three Illinois Arts Council Fellowship Awards, and a National Endowment for the Arts Midwest Regional Fellowship. Pinney was selected for three documentary projects that were exhibited, published, and archived in Chicago: Changing Chicago (1987), City 2000, and most recently, her work in the Chicago Public Schools. Pinney’s first monograph, Regarding Emma: Photographs of American Women and Girls (2003) was followed by Girl Ascending (2010), TWO (2015), and In Their Own Light: Photographs from Chicago Public Schools (2023).Recent exhibitions include The Outwin 2022: American Portraiture Today, at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery, Go Down Moses at the Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2019), A History of Photography, at the George Eastman Museum (2019 and 2023), Girl Transcendent at the Schneider International Gallery, Maui (2018), Photographs from the Collection, at the Art Institute of Chicago (2018), American Photographs, 1845 to Now, at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art (2017); The Gender Show, at the Fundación Canal, Madrid, Spain (2016), and Girls on the Verge: Portraits of Adolescence at the Art Institute of Chicago, 2008.Pinney’s photographs are in the collections of the Art Institute of Chicago, George Eastman Museum, J. Paul Getty Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Museum of Fine Arts Houston, Museum of Modern Art, International Center of Photography, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Whitney Museum of American Art, among others. About the ICP Incubator SpaceICP’s Incubator Space is a new exhibition program designed to highlight the work of emerging photographers who are responding in real time to the world around us. ICP will present a rotating selection of projects by imagemakers experimenting with and pushing boundaries around the documentary tradition. ICP’s Incubator Space is curated by Sara Ickow, Associate Director of Exhibitions at ICP.

candidates.text: ​Grounded: Picture a Tree From the F Train-adjacent house in Gravesend, Brooklyn that serves as his headquarters, Paul Graviano has molded his life and business around the art and philosophy of bonsai. Evolving a hobby and vast personal collection into a 40-year career growing and shaping miniature trees, Graviano spent time working with legendary bonsai expert Frank Okamura while volunteering at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden before founding the Bonsai of Brooklyn in 1976 – one of the oldest businesses in the U.S. dedicated to the Japanese bonsai tradition. - Tony Blahd Now in his eighties, Graviano reflects on the landscape of memory, and a life deeply influenced by plants for the short documentary Picture a Tree , directed by Tony Blahd. First connecting in 2017 while sourcing bonsai trees for another project, Blahd found himself in Graviano's office, where soil-dusted carpets, and walls hung with bonsai tools and ephemera, compete with a miniature train set – complete with a massive scale model of his Brooklyn neighborhood – that occupies the basement. Returning to capture his world, and the patience and dedication demanded from bonsai cultivation, Picture a Tree weaves new interviews and archive footage into an exploration of the ways plants relate to creativity, philosophy, and ways of living, building a spirited ode to botanical obsession and Graviano’s quiet fascination with life in miniature.

candidates.text: In On Rape and Institutional Failure, an exhibition centered on the second chapter of her ongoing project A History of Misogyny, Laia Abril examines different forms of violence against women throughout history.Weaving together images, compiled testimonies, archival materials, select objects, and installations with sound and video, the exhibition investigates how gender-based stereotypes, coupled with worldwide prejudices and misconceptions, have contributed to a systemic rape culture that persists today. By focusing on institutions, Abril aims to avoid narratives of victim-blaming, instead addressing the on-going problem of social accountability that has allowed offenders and enablers alike to avoid justice. On Rape and Institutional Failure was first exhibited in 2020 in the wake of the initial, galvanizing allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other powerful men. While #MeToo has led to few sustained consequences and little systemic change, Abril offers a meaningful opportunity to address the long history of silencing victims and the transgenerational trauma that has developed as a result. candidates.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reconsiders and expands on the history of Japanese photography through the work twenty-eight intergenerational artists from the 1950s to today. Presented in partnership with Aperture and curated by Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko, the exhibition includes work by Fujioka Aya, Hara Mikiko, Hiromix, Ishikawa Mao, Ishiuchi Miyako, Katayama Mari, Kawauchi Rinko, Komatsu Hiroko, Kon Michiko, Nagashima Yurie, Narahashi Asako, Ninagawa Mika, Nishimura Tamiko, Noguchi Rika, Nomura Sakiko, Okabe Momo, Okanoue Toshiko, Onodera Yuki, Sawada Tomoko, Shiga Lieko, Sugiura Kunié, Suzuki Nozomi, Tawada Yuki, Tokiwa Toyoko, Ushioda Tokuko, Watanabe Hitomi, Yamazawa Eiko and Yanagi Miwa.Spanning photography, installation, photobooks, and printed matter, the exhibition explores the experiences and perspectives of women in Japan through delicate and blunt observations of everyday life, critical reflections on the roles inhabited and reshaped by Japanese women, and approaches that push the boundaries of photography. The exhibition is accompanied by a major publication (Aperture, 2024) that expands upon content of the show through essays, historical material, and a comprehensive bibliography of photobooks made by Japanese women.I'm So Happy You Are Here is an exhibition with a strong international pedigree. Following its debut at Rencontres d’Arles, France (2024), the exhibition has traveled to The Hague (2024), Frankfurt (2025), London (2026), and Tokyo (2026), before arriving at ICP for its first US showing here in New York.Financial Times | Arles: “The highlight” of Rencontres d’Arles.W Magazine | London: “The Japanese Women Who Rewrote Photography’s Rules.”Time Out Tokyo | Tokyo: “The exhibition offers a vital counter-narrative to a photographic canon long dominated by male figures.” About Curators:Lesley A. Martin is executive director of Printed Matter. Most recently, she was the creative director of Aperture, where she served as editor on more than one hundred books on photography, and as founding publisher of The PhotoBook Review. Takeuchi Mariko is a photography critic, curator, and professor at Kyoto University of the Arts. Previously, she served as visiting researcher at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, and at the National Museum of Art, Osaka. Pauline Vermare is the Phillip and Edith Leonian Curator, Photography, Brooklyn Museum. Previously, she served as the cultural director of Magnum Photos in New York, and curator at the International Center of Photography and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. About Aperture:Aperture is a nonprofit publisher that leads conversations around photography worldwide. From its new home opening this September in New York, Aperture connects global audiences and supports artists through its acclaimed quarterly magazine, books, exhibitions, digital platforms, public programs, limited-edition prints, and awards. Established in 1952 to advance “creative thinking, significantly expressed in words and photographs,” Aperture champions photography’s vital role in nurturing curiosity and encouraging a more just, tolerant society. For more information, visit aperture.org Header image: Kawauchi Rinko, Untitled, 2004; from the series the eyes, the ears. Courtesy the artist and Aperture

candidates.text: Raw Materials: Diego Delgado-Elias Drawn to historic buildings and the traces they carry, Peruvian designer and architect Diego Delgado-Elias has spent his 20-year career reinforcing the elements that develop a space’s warmth and character. Based in Paris, his architecture and interior design studio expands this affinity for creating lived-in spaces that seem to have accumulated naturally over time, observing the lives that occupied a house before him – left as marks on walls, layers of paint, or objects that appear frozen and unmoved. - Daniel Guix While working to restore a seventeenth-century house in the Provençal village of Visan, France, Delgado-Elias found a place that quietly mirrors his sentimental understanding and way of looking at spaces. Moving between past and present, the house becomes an echo of other spaces and sensations that remain with him, while bearing the influence of the surrounding nature in its preserved frescoes, original materials, and domestic objects. For a new short documentary, director Daniel Guix studies Delgado-Elias’ world through the house, exploring how our earliest encounters with spaces can mold our sensibility. Shooting on 16mm, to capture the grain, movement and texture of memory, Guix brings Delgado-Elias’ reflections into conversation with the house, as a rhythm that connects one room to the next, and a reminder of the formative impressions that unconsciously shape creative vision.
candidates.title: Raw Materials: Diego Delgado-Elias
